html:
The Wieliczka Salt Mine near Kraków was dug from the 1200s and worked for over 700 years, and its rock salt was one of the main sources of income of the Polish kings.

With the nearby Bochnia mine it formed the royal salt works, which in the time of Casimir the Great provided a large part of the crown's revenue. Its tunnels run for about 300 kilometres on nine levels. Miners carved chapels, statues and chandeliers from the salt, the largest being the Chapel of Saint Kinga. Visitors such as Copernicus and Goethe came. Commercial mining ended in 1996 due to flooding and low prices. It was among the first places on the World Heritage list in 1978, and it shows how salt built wealth before refrigeration.
